lines: Morgan Patel
+1 (555) 010-4410 | morgan.patel@example.com | example.com/code/mpatel
EDUCATION
Ridgeway University | Ph.D. candidate in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2021 - Expected May 2026
Ridgeway University | B.S. in Mathematics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Sunrise Bakery | Assistant Store Manager | Metro City, USA | Sep 2025 - Present
- Managed opening shifts and a team of 6 bakers and cashiers, keeping the store within its weekly labour budget.
- Ran daily stock counts and supplier orders, cutting unsold bread from 12% to 7% of production.
Northpeak Capital | Quantitative Research Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2025 - Aug 2025
- Improved risk-adjusted returns by 35% with a cost-aware position smoother on the desk's futures signal.
- Validated the signal on 6 years of tick data with purged walk-forward splits and an embargo period, so every backtest decision used only information available at the time.
- Wrote a feature store for 120 microstructure features with point-in-time joins, which the research team reused in two later signal projects.
- Presented the signal, its capacity estimate and failure cases to the portfolio managers, who approved a small live allocation for the next quarter.
- Selected the smoother's parameters from 400 backtested configurations and reported the best one's Sharpe as the expected live Sharpe.
- Built a short-horizon order-book imbalance signal for liquid index futures that raised the desk book's Sharpe ratio from 1.1 to 1.5 over 18 months of out-of-sample backtest after costs.
Ridgeway University | Research Assistant, Statistical Learning Lab | Metro City, USA | Jun 2020 - Aug 2021
- Cut a 2,000-run Monte Carlo study from 3 days to 5 hours by running the runs in parallel with the same random seed on every worker.
- Derived a variance bound for a sparse regression estimator; my proof tightens the previous bound by a log factor and is now Section 3 of a paper under review at JASA.
- Taught weekly recitations for 60 students in graduate probability, writing 12 problem sets and earning a 4.8/5 teaching rating.
- Released an open-source R package for high-dimensional covariance estimation with shrinkage and factor models, downloaded 3,000 times in its first year.
PROJECTS
Volatility Forecasting Study | Independent Research | Python, PyTorch | Jan 2024 - Present
- Beat a HAR-RV baseline's out-of-sample QLIKE loss by 7% on 30 equity indices with a temporal convolutional model trained on realized-volatility features.
- Tested significance with Diebold-Mariano tests across the 30 indices; after a Holm correction the forecast gain held at the 5% level on 24 of them and in both crisis periods.
- Wrote up the method, robustness checks and results as a 12-page working paper, which was presented at the department's financial econometrics seminar.
Kaggle Market Prediction Competition | Team of 3 | Python | Mar 2023 - Jun 2023
- Engineered features and trained gradient-boosting models for a market prediction competition.
- Cut validation leakage by switching to time-grouped folds, which closed a 0.02 gap between local validation and leaderboard scores.
- Added 0.4 to the Sharpe ratio of a futures book with an order-book imbalance signal, tested over 18 months out of sample.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, R, PyTorch, Kafka
Methods: time-series econometircs, high-dimensional statistics, gradient boosting

items.says: The résumé does not make its target role clear.
items.because: It is highly quantitative and finance-oriented, but the bakery role is prominent and there is no summary or target-role indication.

items.says: Make the technical experience more visually dominant.
items.because: The current bakery role receives space that may be more valuable for the technical background.

items.says: Check bullets that wrap awkwardly in the final PDF.
Standardize capitalization, punctuation, and date formatting.
Verify that the code URL is complete and functional.
items.because: The repository should contain the projects and packages mentioned in the résumé.

items.says: Consider adding a current, consistent professional profile.
Replace placeholder-looking contact details in the submitted résumé.
items.because: Anonymized details are fine for review, but not for submission.

items.says: Clarify what “Ph.D. candidate” means for your academic status.
items.because: Some employers take it to mean qualifying exams are complete, while others use it loosely.

items.says: Add a relevant research area, dissertation topic, or specialization.
items.because: The experience spans statistical learning, financial econometrics, and quantitative finance.

items.says: Keep the expected completion date current and credible.
items.because: The timeline may change.

items.says: Check the degree titles and their reverse-chronological presentation.
Include notable honors, distinction, or a relevant concentration if useful.
Reduce the space given to the bakery role for technical applications.
items.because: That space may be more valuable for the technical background.

items.says: Clarify the scope of managing a team of six.
items.because: They could be direct reports, people scheduled per shift, or everyone working under you.

items.says: Quantify the budget result if possible.
items.because: “Keeping within budget” is less persuasive than a measurable improvement or consistent result.

items.says: Use U.S. spelling instead of “labour” for U.S. employers.
items.because: It is unusual for a U.S.-based résumé.

items.says: Shorten or deprioritize this bullet for technical applications.
items.because: It shows management and operations but contributes little to the quantitative profile.

items.says: Specify the comparison period and measurement basis for the reduction in unsold bread.
items.because: Employers may wonder whether it was temporary, seasonal, or sustained.

items.says: Verify the denominator and attribution of the reduction.
items.because: “Of production” must be the correct denominator, and broader changes could explain the result.

items.says: Define “risk-adjusted returns.”
items.because: It could refer to Sharpe ratio, information ratio, return divided by volatility, or another metric.

items.says: State the comparison basis and evaluation period.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether the result was in-sample, out-of-sample, simulated, or live.

items.says: Clarify which costs, market impact, and capacity were included.
Explain the relationship between the 35% result and the later Sharpe-ratio claim.
items.because: They may describe the same work, but the relationship is unclear.

items.says: Make “position smoother” and “desk’s futures signal” clear to the intended audience.
items.because: They are domain-specific terms.

items.says: Qualify the claim that every backtest decision used only available information.
items.because: That is broader than saying the splits were purged and had an embargo.

items.says: Add the number of folds or evaluation windows if useful.
items.because: It could demonstrate rigor.

items.says: Reconcile the validation claim with selection from 400 configurations.
items.because: Many trials can leak information across evaluation decisions even when individual folds are time-aware.

items.says: Clarify ownership and the feature store’s scale.
items.because: Employers may care about data volume, latency, productionization, or testing.

items.says: Name the technology used to build the feature store.
items.because: Kafka alone does not establish whether it used SQL, Spark, cloud infrastructure, or another stack.

items.says: Link the feature-store work if confidentiality permits.
Verify that the allocation and investment-process information can be disclosed.
items.because: It may reveal confidential internal processes or results.

items.says: Clarify your role in approval and deployment.
items.because: “Who approved” can make the investment decision sound like your contribution rather than the presentation of research.

items.says: Clarify “small live allocation” if disclosure rules permit.
items.because: The scale language is not very informative.

items.says: Reporting the best of 400 backtested Sharpes as expected live Sharpe is not statistically defensible.
items.because: It introduces selection bias and likely backtest overfitting without an independent validation procedure.

items.says: The order-book signal result appears duplicated in the Kaggle project.
items.because: Both claims use an 18-month out-of-sample period and nearly identical performance framing.

items.says: Clarify the baseline and attribution of the Sharpe increase.
items.because: It is unclear whether 1.1 and 1.5 describe the desk book with and without the signal or different model configurations.

items.says: Specify whether all 18 months were held out from development.
Qualify “raised” as a simulated backtest improvement.
items.because: A backtest does not necessarily show a realized or causal improvement.

items.says: Using the same random seed on every worker may undermine the Monte Carlo study.
items.because: Workers may generate identical or correlated simulations instead of independent runs.

items.says: State the parallelization environment if relevant.
items.because: Employers could then see whether the work used multiprocessing, a cluster, cloud computing, or a specific framework.

items.says: Clarify authorship and your contribution to the proof.
items.because: The work may be collaborative.

items.says: Emphasize the mathematical contribution rather than “now Section 3.”
items.because: The section number is less useful to a recruiter than the result’s significance.

items.says: Use the journal’s exact official name or a consistent accepted abbreviation.
Add a publication or preprint link if available.
Specify the source or response basis of the 4.8/5 rating.
items.because: A small response pool differs from a full-class evaluation.

items.says: Give teaching less space than research for research or industry applications unless relevant.
Add the package name and a link if publicly available.
Clarify what the 3,000 downloads count measures.
items.because: Repository counts can include automated downloads.

items.says: Consider stronger adoption evidence than raw download count.
items.because: Tests, documentation, users, citations, or downstream adoption may be stronger indicators.

items.says: Make the “Independent Research” label consistent with your academic status.
items.because: The project overlaps the Ph.D. period and may instead be dissertation or university research.

items.says: Explain that lower QLIKE is better.
items.because: Not every reader knows how to interpret the metric.

items.says: Specify the forecast horizon and evaluation period.
Replace the informal word “Beat.”
items.because: Terminology should be consistent with the rest of the résumé.

items.says: Clarify whether the model and baseline used identical information sets and evaluation windows.
Clarify what “in both crisis periods” applies to.
items.because: It could mean significance for all 24 indices in each period or an aggregate result.

items.says: Explain how dependence across indices and repeated crisis-period testing were handled.
items.because: A sophisticated reader may question the statistical procedure.

items.says: Link the working paper if it is public.
Clarify whether you were the sole author.
Consider replacing the page count with more useful publication context.
items.because: The paper’s status, audience, or availability matters more.

items.says: Identify the Kaggle competition and its outcome.
items.because: The entry lacks a competition name, ranking, dataset scale, and final result.

items.says: Consider removing the Kaggle project if it has no meaningful external result.
items.because: It is weaker than the rest of the résumé and could give way to more relevant research.

items.says: Make the modeling bullet less generic with a concrete result or scale.
items.because: It gives no feature count, objective, ranking, or measurable improvement.

items.says: Define the 0.02 metric and how the gap changed.
items.because: The local score may have fallen, the leaderboard score may have risen, or both.

items.says: Explain why the original folds leaked information.
Use “closed” only if the gap actually disappeared.
items.because: If it merely narrowed, the wording should give the actual change.

items.says: The order-book signal result appears duplicated in the Northpeak entry.
items.because: It has nearly the same 18-month out-of-sample period and performance framing.

items.says: Distinguish this work from the Northpeak signal if it was separate.
items.because: Different data, dates, instruments, or methodology would make that clear.

items.says: Clarify the baseline Sharpe and treatment of costs, capacity, and selection effects.
Explain the chronology relative to the Northpeak internship.
items.because: The Kaggle project predates the internship, yet the same signal appears as internship work.

items.says: Separate languages from frameworks and infrastructure tools.
items.because: Python and R are languages, while PyTorch and Kafka are tools or platforms.

items.says: Include important tools used in the experience bullets if applicable.
items.because: The list does not identify potentially relevant tools such as SQL, Git, Linux, cloud platforms, or distributed computing.

items.says: Demonstrate meaningful Kafka use elsewhere on the résumé.
items.because: Kafka is unusual in this list without evidence of its use in a project.

items.says: “Econometircs” is misspelled.
Use consistent capitalization and naming conventions.
Expand the methods list to reflect the work shown elsewhere.
items.because: The résumé evidences time-series validation, volatility modeling, Monte Carlo methods, sparse regression, covariance estimation, microstructure features, and statistical testing.

items.says: Reconsider the emphasis on “gradient boosting” relative to other methods.
items.because: Point-in-time handling, purged cross-validation, and multiple-testing correction may be more valuable for the target roles.
